notes.meaning: Ezekiel receives a message from the Lord in the tenth year of exile, in early 587 BC. This was about one year into the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem, just months before the city fell. God speaks right when Israel is tempted to look elsewhere for help.

God tells Ezekiel to look toward Pharaoh, the ruler of Egypt, and speak against him and his whole country. Egypt had often seemed like a powerful friend, but it had repeatedly drawn God's people away from trusting the Lord. Now God makes clear that Egypt will face divine judgment.

Pharaoh is compared to a giant water monster, like a crocodile, resting proudly in the streams of the Nile River. He arrogantly boasts that the Nile belongs to him and that he made it for himself. Forgetting God often leads proud leaders into treating themselves as gods.

God warns that He will put iron hooks into Pharaoh's jaws and haul him right out of his rivers. The fish in the streams will cling to the crocodile's scales and be dragged out as well. This shows that both the ruler of Egypt and the people who rely on him will be pulled into ruin together.

The Lord will throw Pharaoh and his supporters onto the dry desert ground, where water creatures cannot survive. Their fallen bodies will not be gathered for an honorable burial in a tomb, but will be eaten by birds and wild beasts. God brings down even the proudest rulers who think they are untouchable.

God reveals that Egypt was nothing more than a fragile walking stick made of Nile river reeds for Israel. Whenever God's people leaned on Egypt for military help, the reed snapped, tearing their shoulders and wrenching their backs. Leaning on human promises instead of God only brings pain and disappointment.

The Lord declares that He will send an invading army like a sword against Egypt to cut down people and cattle alike. Both the population and their livestock will suffer the blows of war. Human pride cannot protect a nation when God brings judgment.

Egypt's fertile river valley will become a desolate wasteland so the people will finally recognize that the Lord is God. This ruin comes directly because Pharaoh claimed that the Nile was his own creation. God will not share His glory with human rulers who boast in their own works.

God sets Himself against Pharaoh and his river canals across the entire nation. He promises to make the whole country a waste from Migdol in the far north to Syene in the south, all the way to the border of Cush. No corner of Egypt will escape this complete devastation.

Neither human traveler nor domestic animal will pass through the devastated land for forty years. It will lie quiet and empty for a full generation of discipline. God often uses seasons of trial to teach nations and people their true weakness.

differ.view: The forty years is a symbolic number representing a fixed time of divine discipline and political weakness, rather than an exact historical count.
The forty years should be taken literally as an actual period of historical desolation, even if secular Egyptian records do not record it.

notes.meaning: Egypt will be ruined just like other conquered nations, and its cities will sit empty for forty years. The Egyptians themselves will be marched away into exile and scattered across foreign lands. God shows that no world empire can stand above His sovereign will.

After forty years have passed, the Lord promises to gather the scattered Egyptians back from the lands where they were taken. Unlike many other ancient powers, Egypt receives a direct promise of national return. God shows surprising mercy even to nations that once opposed Him.

God promises to bring the captives back to Pathros in southern Egypt, the original cradle of their civilization. Yet Egypt will only be a lowly, second-rate kingdom that will never rule over other nations again. God humbles great world empires so they cannot boast or oppress others anymore.

The restored kingdom will never again tempt Israel to put its faith in Egyptian chariots and armies. Instead, Egypt's weakened state will serve as an ongoing reminder of how foolish it was to look to humans for rescue. God wants His people to rely on Him alone for their security.

Another message came to Ezekiel on the first day of the year in the twenty-seventh year of exile, around 571 BC. This is the latest date given anywhere in the book, coming about sixteen years after the previous prophecy. God speaks right on time to fulfill every promise He has made.

God explains that King Nebuchadnezzar made his Babylonian soldiers work hard through a thirteen-year siege against the island city of Tyre. Their heads grew bald from helmets and their shoulders were rubbed raw from carrying heavy stones, yet they found little treasure because Tyre sailed its wealth away. Long and painful earthly labor often leaves people empty-handed.

God announces that He is handing Egypt over to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for the hard labor his army performed at Tyre. The Babylonians were unaware that they were serving God's purpose, yet the Lord saw their work and gave them Egypt's plunder as their pay. God faithfully settles every account and directs all world events.

God promises to cause a horn of strength and new life to sprout for Israel during that season of restoration. Ezekiel would also be able to speak freely among his people, because everyone would finally see that his words were true. God restores the dignity of His people and confirms the truth of His word.

differ.view: The budding horn points ahead to the coming Messiah, Jesus Christ, who brings full strength and redemption to God's people.
The horn refers directly to the renewal of strength and encouragement for the Jewish people when God judged Egypt, rather than the Messiah.
